content.title: About
content.content: Beef and vegetables, Hawaiian style is a dish that combines tender strips of beef, fresh vegetables (bell pepper, carrot, pineapple) and a fragrant sauce made from soy sauce, ginger and coconut milk. It cooks quickly, retains bright flavors and evokes the tropical culinary vibe of Hawaii.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional Hawaiian cooking often uses pineapple, which adds a sweet note and helps tenderize meat.
Beef marinated in soy sauce and ginger absorbs flavors faster, a technique common in poke dishes.
The dish is frequently served over rice or noodles, but the original Hawaiian version is eaten with leafy greens.
The sweet‑salty balance (pineapple and soy sauce) reflects the harmony of flavors typical of Hawaiian cuisine.
Hawaiian chefs usually use vegetables harvested the same day to keep a crisp texture.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beef provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat supplies vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Antioxidants from vegetables
items.content: Bell pepper and carrot are rich in vitamin C and carotenoids, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Benefits of coconut milk
items.content: Coconut milk contains medium‑chain triglycerides that can provide a quick energy source.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Fatty cuts of beef can raise cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

items.title: Coconut allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to coconut milk.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce adds a significant amount of salt, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked beef may harbor pathogenic bacteria; cook to an internal temperature of 71 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, typically over steamed rice, noodles, or a bed of lettuce. Garnish with fresh pineapple, cilantro and a squeeze of lime for extra brightness. Leftovers store in the fridge and reheat in a skillet or microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly before eating.
